group.title: Phrasal verbs
group.tagline: Bring about, come across, rule out
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To make something happen, especially a change.
examples: The new law {brought about} big changes in schools.
wrong: Her campaign brought about change by stopping anything from happening.

words.meaning: To decide that something is not possible or not suitable.
examples: Police have {ruled out} an accident.
wrong: The doctor ruled out the flu, so she said it was definitely the flu.

words.meaning: To stop yourself from showing a feeling or doing something.
examples: She {held back} her tears during the speech.
wrong: He held back his anger by shouting at everyone.

words.meaning: To move an event to an earlier date or time.
examples: The meeting has been {brought forward} to Monday.
wrong: They brought the exam forward by moving it two weeks later.

words.meaning: To say publicly that something is needed or should happen.
examples: Parents are {calling for} safer roads near the school.
wrong: The group called for a new park by saying nobody needs one.

words.meaning: To offer help or information, especially to the police.
examples: Two witnesses {came forward} after the crash.
wrong: She came forward with information by hiding and saying nothing.

words.meaning: To manage even though you do not have something.
examples: We’ll have to {do without} a car for a while.
wrong: I can’t do without coffee, so I never drink it.

words.meaning: To agree with or accept an idea or plan.
examples: I’ll {go along with} whatever you decide.
wrong: He went along with the plan by refusing to take part.

words.meaning: To become gradually weaker or quieter.
examples: We waited for the wind to {die down}.
wrong: The noise died down until it was louder than ever.

words.meaning: To get better after a serious illness, or survive a hard time.
examples: The doctors think he will {pull through}.
wrong: She pulled through the illness and never recovered.

words.meaning: To make people understand an idea or message.
examples: The ad {gets across} a simple message.
wrong: She got her point across, so nobody understood what she meant.

words.meaning: To choose one person or thing from a group for special attention.
examples: The teacher {singled out} Maria for praise.
wrong: The coach singled out the whole team equally, without picking anyone.

words.meaning: To make something seem less important or serious than it is.
examples: The company {played down} the problem.
wrong: He played down the danger by shouting that it was a disaster.

words.meaning: To stop insisting on something after people oppose you.
examples: After the protest, the council {backed down}.
wrong: He backed down and refused to change his position at all.

words.meaning: To destroy something completely.
examples: The flood {wiped out} the whole crop.
wrong: The disease wiped out the population, which grew larger than ever.

words.meaning: To consider all the possible results of a plan carefully.
examples: Have you {thought through} what you’ll do next?
wrong: She thought the plan through by deciding in two seconds without any thought.

words.meaning: To reduce a number of choices to fewer.
examples: We {narrowed down} the list to three hotels.
wrong: They narrowed down the options from five to fifty.

words.meaning: To suggest an idea or plan for people to consider.
examples: She {put forward} a plan to save money.
wrong: He put forward a proposal by keeping it secret from everyone.

words.meaning: To persuade someone to support or like you.
examples: Her honest speech {won over} the audience.
wrong: He won over the voters, so they all turned against him.

words.meaning: To explain the reason for something, or to form a part of a total.
examples: Bad weather {accounts for} the late trains.
wrong: Students account for half the town’s population, so there are hardly any students.

words.meaning: To stop taking part in something, or to leave an agreement.
examples: Two teams {pulled out} of the tournament.
wrong: She pulled out of the race and finished in first place.

words.meaning: To decide not to do something you agreed to do.
examples: He {backed out} of the deal at the last minute.
wrong: She backed out of the trip and went on it just as she had promised.

words.meaning: To become popular.
examples: The new dance quickly {caught on} with teenagers.
wrong: The app caught on, so nobody ever used it.

words.meaning: To prepare and write a plan, list or document.
examples: The lawyer {drew up} a new contract.
wrong: They drew up a list without writing anything down.

words.meaning: Of a plan or deal: to fail to happen.
examples: Our holiday plans {fell through} when the flight was canceled.
wrong: The deal fell through, so it went ahead exactly as planned.

words.meaning: To realize that someone is trying to trick you.
examples: She {saw through} his excuses at once.
wrong: He saw through the lie, so he believed every word of it.

words.meaning: To leave an important job or position.
examples: The chairman {stepped down} after twenty years.
wrong: She stepped down as director and stayed in the role.

words.meaning: To give the main points of something in a short form.
examples: To {sum up}, the plan is cheap and quick.
wrong: He summed up the report by reading every page aloud in full.

words.meaning: To notice something that is not obvious.
examples: She {picked up on} the tension in the room.
wrong: He picked up on her mood, so he didn’t notice anything.

words.meaning: To happen, especially in a way that was not planned.
examples: How did this mess {come about}?
wrong: The change came about, so nothing happened.

words.meaning: To appear or happen suddenly and unexpectedly.
examples: A problem {cropped up} just before the launch.
wrong: Something cropped up that we had planned for months.

words.meaning: To accept and deal with a difficult truth or situation.
examples: You need to {face up to} your mistakes.
wrong: He faced up to the problem by pretending it didn’t exist.

words.meaning: Of a feeling or effect: to slowly disappear.
examples: The painkillers {wore off} after a few hours.
wrong: The excitement wore off and grew stronger every day.

words.meaning: Of news or a fact: to become fully understood.
examples: It took a while for the news to {sink in}.
wrong: The bad news sank in, so she still didn’t understand it at all.

words.meaning: To do something good to correct a past problem or loss.
examples: I bought her lunch to {make up for} being late.
wrong: He made up for his rudeness by being rude again.

words.meaning: To admit that you did something wrong.
examples: Nobody {owned up} to breaking the window.
wrong: She owned up to the mistake by blaming her brother.

words.meaning: To make a careless mistake.
examples: The goalkeeper {slipped up} and let in an easy goal.
wrong: She slipped up by doing everything perfectly.

words.meaning: To keep something, like time or money, for a special purpose.
examples: I {set aside} an hour every day for reading.
wrong: She set aside money for the trip by spending it all at once.

words.meaning: To defend or support someone or something that is being attacked.
examples: You should {stand up for} your friends.
wrong: He stood up for his sister by joining the bullies against her.

words.meaning: To be as good as people expected.
examples: The movie didn’t {live up to} the reviews.
wrong: The hotel lived up to our hopes and was a big disappointment.
